messages.subject: Estimating factor scores for bifactor model with NA responses
messages.subject_clean: Estimating factor scores for bifactor model with NA responses
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a mirt object (simmod) for bifactor model. However, when I use NA for the responses except the first response, fscores() estimates latent traits for the other specific factor scores as well. Does it mean constrains passed from simmod does not work? Is there a way to specify constrains again when estimating factor scores?

PS. I am planning to use fscores() function in my own CAT algorithm.

Any help is appreciated, thank you so much!

a <- matrix(0, 12, 4)
a[,1] <- rlnorm(12, .2, .3)
ind <- 1
for(i in 1:3){
  a[ind:(ind+3),i+1] <- a[ind:(ind+3),1]
  ind <- ind+4 }
print(a)
d <- rnorm(12, 0, .5)
guess <- rnorm(12, 0.1, 0.03)
sigma <- diag(c(1, .5, 1, .5))

dataset <- simdata(a=a,d=d, guess =guess, 1000,itemtype=rep('3PL', 12),sigma=sigma)
# estimate by applying constraints and freeing the latent variances
specific <- c(rep(1,4),rep(2,4), rep(3,4))

model <- "G = 1-12
              CONSTRAIN = (1, a1, a2), (2, a1, a2), (3, a1, a2), (4, a1, a2),
                (5, a1, a3), (6, a1, a3), (7, a1, a3), (8, a1, a3),
                (9, a1, a4), (10, a1, a4), (11, a1, a4), (12, a1, a4)
              COV = S1*S1, S2*S2, S3*S3"
simmod <- bfactor(dataset, specific, model, guess=guess)

fscores(object = simmod,
              response.pattern = c(0, rep(NA, 11)),
              method = "EAP",
              quadpts = 61,
              theta_lim = c(-4.5, 4.5),
              QMC = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
61 quasi-quadrature points is much too low for quasi-Monte Carlo integration. You'd need something in the thousands to obtain reasonable accuracy. Increasing your example to 5000 gives the following.

> fs <- fscores(object = simmod,
+         response.pattern = c(0, rep(NA, 11)),
+         method = "EAP",
+         quadpts = 5000,
+         theta_lim = c(-4.5, 4.5),
+         QMC = TRUE)
> round(fs, 3)
             G       S1 S2 S3  SE_G SE_S1 SE_S2 SE_S3
[1,] -0.248 -0.248   0    0 0.965    0.965          1    0.999

Though in all honesty, you're likely better off using modal estimates like MAP as they don't have numerical integration problems at all. The SEs will be a little off early on in the session, but as the number of items increase MAP and EAP information converge towards the same estimates. HTH.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: Starting values for mixture IRT models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Shelley,

Mixture models can be tricky, and are often prone to local minimum issues. When you fit these models do the final log-likelihood values differ? If so, you likely have local min problems, and should consider what you are seeing (even when picking the 'most likely' model) with some skepticism as there are multiple good ways to fit the same data under the same model. From my experience whenever the mixture model has difficulty converging it is because the mixtures are not sufficiently identifiable, and though they may exist the data does not allow for their structure to be stably detected. And yes, the GenRandomPars=TRUE argument is effectively the same as what MPlus does in the same model.

For your question 2), you can pass pars = 'values' to see how the starting values look, and if you like feel free to modify this data.frame of values and re-supply it to the pars input to use something you believe is better. HTH.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Dear Phil,

I fit four models to the operational data of an English language proficiency test using both R package mirt and BMIRT Toolkit (Yao,2003, 2013[1]). The models include unidimensional IRT, uncorrelated factor multidimensional IRT, correlated factor multidimensional IRT, and bifactor. Surprisingly, the AIC and BIC values obtained from the two programs were different (please see Table 2 in the attachments). While, based on mirt, bifactor model had the best and uncorrelated MIRT had the worst fit, in BMIRT unidimensional model had the best and bifactor model had the worst fit. Considering that I rechecked the steps in doing the analyses and ran the analyses several times to make sure I haven’t made a mistake, how can this difference be explained?

I’d be grateful if you could help me with this.

Best regards,

Mohammad

Yao, L. (2013). The BMIRT toolkit. Monterey. https://www.bmirt.com/8220.html

messages.body_plain:
Hi Phil,

I'm trying to adapt/simulate a personality test (14 distinct, but intercorrelated dimensions from 210 polytomous items) as a CAT from real data in 3 steps. My goal is to study the efficiency of CAT in comparison to linear testing for this questionnaire.

First I interpreted each dimension as an unidimensional factor, separated the items into 14 different datasets, fitted 14 unidimensional GRM-models and administered 14 independent UCATs. Up to this point, that worked well: The UCATs need only around 50% of the items in average.

Now second I want to run an MCAT with all 14 dimensions and the compete dataset, but uncorrelated, so as to compare the results to step 1. I fitted a mirt-model like this:

model <- 'F1 =  7, 22, 37, 53, 69, 85, 100, 115, 130, 144, 159, 172, 196, 204

                 F2 =  8, 23, 38, 54, 70, 86, 101, 116, 131, 145, 173, 186

                 F3 =  9, 24, 39, 55, 71, 87, 102, 117, 132, 146, 160, 174, 187, 197, 205

                 F4 =  11, 26, 41, 57, 73, 89, 104, 119, 134, 148, 162, 176, 188, 206

                 F5 =  12, 27, 42, 58, 74, 90, 105, 120, 135, 149, 163, 177, 189, 198

                 F6 =  13, 28, 43, 59, 75, 91, 106, 121, 136, 150, 164, 178, 190, 199

                 F7 =  14, 29, 44, 60, 76, 92, 107, 122, 151, 165, 179, 191

                 F8 =  2, 16, 31, 46, 62, 78, 94, 109, 124, 138, 153, 167, 181, 192, 201, 208

                 F9=  1, 15, 30, 45, 61, 77, 93, 108, 123, 137, 152, 166, 180, 200, 207

                 F10 =  3, 17, 32, 47, 63, 79, 95, 110, 125, 139, 154, 168, 182

                 F11 =  10, 25, 40, 56, 72, 88, 103, 118, 133, 147, 161, 175

                 F12 =  4, 18, 33, 48, 64, 80, 96, 111, 126, 140, 155, 169, 183, 193, 202, 209

                 F13 =  5, 19, 34, 49, 65, 81, 97, 112, 127, 141, 156, 170, 184

                 F14 =  6, 20, 35, 50, 66, 82, 98, 113, 128, 142, 157, 171, 185, 194, 203, 210'

Generated the mirt-model like:

mirt.model <- mirt(data, model = model, 'graded', cl = cl, method = "MHRM")

And ran the MCAT like this:

cat.design <- list(min_items = 5, min_SEM = 0.35, delta_thetas = 0.05) #Same as in UCATs

result <- mirtCAT(mo = mirt.model, local_pattern = data.pattern, start_item = 'Drule', criteria = 'Drule', design = cat.design)

Yet, the thetas of the MCAT for each factor are not remotely comparable to the results of the different UCATs from step 1. There are only around 20 items from 210 selected, SE is quite high (NOT around .35 as wanted). I would have guessed the MCAT would work quite similar to a bunch of UCATs when the factors are treated as uncorrelated. Can you spot my mistake? Is there a way to tell mirtCAT to use the termination criteria (like min_item = 5) for each factor separately?

Then for step 3, I want to repeat the MCAT but with respect to the intercorrelations of the dimensions. As those are quite highly correlated, I expect an even better efficiency in comparison to step 1 and 2. How can I include the intercorrelations into my model? I assume something like 'COV = F1*F2*...*F14' in the model definition - is that correct? Is there a possibility to tell mirt specific correlations/covarinces (for example as a cov-matrix)?

Additionally, I am quite confused with the selection-criteria argument in mirtCAT. With UCATs I use 'MI' for maximum information - which criteria should I use equivalently in MCAT? Is there any literature where I can read about the differences of Drule, Trule, APrule etc.?

I would be very thankful for your help!

Best wishes

Nick
